article.title: A Fire Rescue Gift for My Child: A Father's Hope for Papua's Forests
article.description: A personal reflection by Michael Gilroy Jitmau, connecting a child's Fire Rescue gift and a Netherlands football booklet with the history of Dutch administration in Papua and hopes for the next generation.
article.dek: A simple Fire Rescue toy and a football booklet featuring the Netherlands become the starting point for a father's reflection on Papua's history, identity, and future.
article.intro: Today, I look at a Fire Rescue toy I gave to my child. To a child, it may simply be a little fire engine to play with. But as a father, it reminds me of something much bigger: the forests of Papua and the lives, wildlife, and communities that need protection when fires break out. I am Michael Gilroy Jitmau, and this is a personal reflection inspired by a simple gift.

sections.heading: When a Small Toy Reminds Me of a Bigger Problem
paragraphs: Papua is home to remarkable forests and biodiversity. These forests are important not only for wildlife, but also for communities whose lives and livelihoods are connected to the land. Forest and land fires can damage vegetation, threaten animal habitats, affect air quality, and disrupt people's daily lives.

The figures reported in November 2026 show why this issue deserves attention. BMKG monitoring reported 173 fire points across eight regencies in four provinces of Tanah Papua as of 13 November 2026. Merauke in South Papua accounted for 153 of those reported points. A satellite-detected hotspot or fire point is an indication that needs field verification; it should not automatically be treated as a confirmed fire on the ground.

BNPB reporting on 15 November 2026 also described a cumulative 436 hectares of land affected by fires in South Papua, with around 95 hectares still undergoing suppression at that reporting time. These figures describe a specific reporting period and may change as monitoring and verification continue.

sections.heading: The Meaning I See in a Fire Rescue Toy
paragraphs: When I gave my child this Fire Rescue toy, I wanted to give a simple gift that could bring happiness. The little fire engine represents people who respond when others are in danger. It also reminds me that courage is not only about facing a fire after it starts. Courage can mean preventing a fire before it spreads.

I hope my child will grow up understanding that protecting the environment is a responsibility we share. A toy cannot put out a real forest fire, but it can become a starting point for a conversation about helping others, caring for nature, and taking responsibility.

sections.heading: The Netherlands in the Booklet, and in Papua's History
paragraphs: The football booklet in the photograph features Virgil van Dijk in the colours of the Netherlands. Van Dijk is simply the visual link that made me think about the Netherlands. What interests me here is not football statistics or a player's career, but the long and complicated history between the Netherlands and Papua.

Dutch colonial administration in western New Guinea developed over time. A chapter published by the Australian National University describes Dutch control being established in the western part of New Guinea in the late nineteenth century. In 1898, the Dutch established two government centres on the western side of the island: Manokwari and Fakfak. These places are part of the historical record of Dutch administration in Papua.

When Indonesia received recognition of its sovereignty from the Netherlands in 1949, the status of western New Guinea was not settled with the rest of the former Netherlands East Indies. The Netherlands continued to administer the territory, while Indonesia and the Netherlands disputed its future. During the 1950s and early 1960s, political developments also took place among Papuans. The New Guinea Council was established in 1961, and Papuan political leaders and groups expressed different views about the territory's future. Their perspectives were not all the same, and the period should not be reduced to a single opinion.

On 15 August 1962, Indonesia and the Netherlands signed the New York Agreement. Under that agreement, the administration was transferred from the Netherlands to the United Nations Temporary Executive Authority (UNTEA) on 1 October 1962. The United Nations administered the territory during the transition, before transferring administration to Indonesia on 1 May 1963.

The 1962 agreement also provided for an act of self-determination before the end of 1969. The process that became known as the Act of Free Choice, or Pepera, remains a deeply contested part of Papua's history. The United Nations documented the process under its mandate, while historical scholarship has raised questions about the degree of participation and freedom available to Papuans. A responsible account should acknowledge both the formal agreement and the continuing debate about how the process was carried out.

For me, these dates are more than entries in a history book. They remind me that Papua has a history that deserves to be studied carefully, including the decisions made about its future and the voices of Papuans who lived through those changes. The image of a Dutch football captain on a child's booklet is only a small visual detail; it is the history of Papua that gives this detail a deeper meaning.

sections.heading: Why Forest Fire Prevention Matters in Papua
paragraphs: Preventing forest and land fires requires cooperation. People should avoid using fire carelessly to clear land, never leave burning materials unattended, and report smoke or flames quickly to local authorities. Monitoring and early response are important because a small fire can become much harder to control when it spreads.

Government agencies, local communities, customary leaders, emergency responders, and environmental organizations all have roles to play. Reliable information also matters: satellite detections should be checked on the ground, and updates should clearly identify the location, date, and status of each incident.

sections.heading: The Future I Hope My Child Will See
paragraphs: As a father, I want my child to grow up in a place where forests are still green, the air is clean, and wildlife continues to have a home. I do not want the next generation to know Papua's forests only through old photographs and stories about what once existed.

I hope children in Papua learn from an early age that caring for nature begins with everyday choices. They do not all need to become firefighters. They can become people who refuse to start fires carelessly, speak up when they see danger, and respect the environment around them.

article.closing:
I gave my child a small Fire Rescue toy. It may become one of the memories of childhood, but for me it is also a reminder of what we must protect.

Papua's forests are part of the inheritance we leave to our children. We may not be able to solve every environmental problem alone, but we can begin with awareness, prevention, and the lessons we teach at home.

I want my child to have a happy childhood, and I hope that when they grow up, Papua will still have forests they can see, breathe beside, and feel proud to protect.

— Michael Gilroy Jitmau
